newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS - Malaysia futures exchanges grow, may merge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Malaysia futures exchanges grow, may merge.

text.p: Malaysia's youthful futures exchanges are seeing increased volume as cash markets are whipped by volatility, but a lack of resources may pave the way for the three bourses to merge, market regulators said.

Munir Majid, chairman of the Securities Commission (SC), said on Monday that he was urging the country's commodities, stock and money market futures exchanges to consider merging to save costs and avoid duplication of resources.

In a speech at a derivatives conference, Munir said there were compelling reasons for a merger between the Malaysia Monetary Exchange (MME), which trades interest rate futures, and the Kuala Lumpur Commodity Exchange (KLCE), which trades futures contracts in palm oil, rubber, tin and other commodities.

A third futures exchange, the Kuala Lumpur Options and Financial Futures Exchange Bhd (KLOFFE), trades a futures contract based on the blue chip stock based Composite Index. It also plans to offer options contracts.

"A single exchange for all futures markets in Malaysia would make eminent sense too, as there will be significant economies of scale to be achieved from pooled resources and operations," Munir said in his speech.

After some teething problems, the youngest of the futures exchanges -- KLOFFE and MME -- are seeing a pickup in demand. KLOFFE was begun in December 1995 and MME is a year old. The KLCE was started in 1980.
Roiled by spillover turbulence in Thailand's currency and stock markets, volumes in Malaysian stocks and interest rates futures contracts shot up last week.

Turnover last Friday on the Malaysia Monetary Exchange's (MME) three-month KLIBOR interest rate futures was a record 1,393 contracts valued at 1.4 billion ringgit ($560 million), Mohd Azwar Mahmud, general manager at the MME, said.

Meanwhile, the Kuala Lumpur Options and Financial Futures Exchange (KLOFFE) posted heavy volume for the spot May contract of 1,965 lots on Friday. The contract is based on the Composite Index, the Malaysian stock market's main blue-chip barometer.
KLOFFE volume in previous months had languished at several hundreds of lots a day.

"I think certainly in the last two months, with the volatility, and with the interest and the volume...increasingly a lot more people are talking about our markets," said John Lee, general manager of KLOFFE, when asked for his outlook.
"I think volume is certainly...likely to increase further," he said.

The futures exchanges are merging their clearing operations. On Monday, the Malaysian Derivatives Clearing House Bhd and the Malaysian Futures Clearing Corp Sdn Bhd announced a memorandum of understanding to establish a single settlement house.
While applauding the move, Munir stopped short of saying the SC would force a merger of the futures exchanges, saying the watchdog group preferred to leave that to market forces.
The exchanges themselves have not said anything about large-scale merger moves.
Munir also said he believes Malaysia may not need many more dervatives exchanges, although the SC as a regulatory body would not restrict the growth of such bourses.

Saying he was expressing personal views, Munir said, "..(I'm) not saying that I would support or indeed would promote the establishment and the existence of multiple derviatives exchanges in Malaysia. With the current state of affairs, there is duplication, and in some cases, triplication, of resources, effort and cost...," he said.
